disclaimer: Proposed alert tiers, not NASA limits. The band is a wellness-grade sensor and this is not a diagnostic device.

profiles.label: Surface rover
profiles.note: Treated as a surface environment, so gravity checks are on. This is an assumption to confirm.

hr.label: 100 bpm: top of the usual resting range

metrics.title: Resting heart rate
metrics.baseline_rule: 7-day median of the heart rate in resting minutes (resting = no motion in the wrist band for at least 10 minutes in a row)

tiers.green: within +/-10% of your baseline AND 50-100 bpm
tiers.yellow: more than 10% off your baseline for at least 30 resting minutes in a row, OR resting below 50 or above 100 for at least 10 minutes
tiers.red: resting above 120 or below 40 for at least 10 minutes, OR an abnormal value together with chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath logged in the last 2 hours

metrics.persistence: 30 min for a change from baseline; 10 min for the absolute limits
metrics.evidence_note: Adult resting 60-100 bpm is a clinical convention. In-flight heart rate tends to run lower, so your own baseline matters more than the absolute numbers.
sources: Adult resting heart rate 60-100 bpm: clinical convention
Long-duration spaceflight heart rate and arterial pressure: https://peeref.com/works/15357458
metrics.limitation: Needs a baseline built from your own resting data. Accuracy depends on band fit and motion, and the tile stays gray until the band has seen you at rest.

action.yellow: Rest, recheck in a few minutes, and review hydration, sleep and stress.
action.red: Tell the crew medical officer / ground medical now.

explain.how: Wear the band snugly. Your resting heart rate is only read when you have been still for about ten minutes, so sit or float quietly now and then.
explain.meaning: Your heart rate while resting, compared with your own usual resting rate. A steady rise or fall can mean stress, poor sleep, illness, dehydration or fatigue.
explain.why: Spaceflight changes how the heart and blood vessels work. Your own trend is the most useful early warning.

metrics.title: Skin temperature
metrics.baseline_rule: your own median for each hour of the day (UTC) over 14 days, leaving out the last 24 hours

tiers.green: within your normal curve for this time of day
tiers.yellow: about 0.5 °C or more above your own curve for the same hour, sustained for 30 minutes (confirm with a thermometer)
tiers.red: only from a core or oral temperature of 38 °C or more that you logged yourself; the band alone is never red

metrics.evidence_note: Wrist skin temperature is not core temperature. Fever is about 38 °C or more measured in the core or mouth.
sources: Core temperature about 36.1-37.8 °C, wrist skin temperature about 33-37 °C
Feasibility of continuous fever monitoring with wearables: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7736301
metrics.limitation: Wrist estimates of core temperature can be off by about -0.7 to +0.9 °C. There is no single absolute wrist limit, so the tile needs about 3 days of your own data first.

action.yellow: Confirm with a thermometer and log the core or oral reading in the Health Log.
action.red: Tell the crew medical officer / ground medical: a core or oral temperature of 38 °C or more.

explain.how: Seat the probe against the inner forearm. For a confirmation, use an oral or core thermometer and log it.
explain.meaning: Compared with your own usual temperature for this time of day. Skin temperature naturally rises and falls over the day, so a single number means little.
explain.why: A sustained rise can be an early sign of infection or heat stress. Spaceflight changes immune function.

metrics.title: Blood oxygen

tiers.yellow: 90-94%: retest at rest and check the fit of the sensor
tiers.red: below 90% on at least 3 one-minute medians in a row, never a single reading

metrics.persistence: 3 consecutive 1-minute medians for red; minutes with motion are skipped
metrics.evidence_note: The 95% and 90% marks are common clinical conventions. The tiers built on them are our own proposal.
sources: Normal SpO2 is 95% or more; below 90% is clinically relevant
Apple Watch SpO2 vs medical oximeter: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9554125
metrics.limitation: A wearable can differ from a medical oximeter by up to about 6% (90-100% range) and 8% (below 90%). Low values are detected reliably on average, but treat a single number with care.

action.yellow: Retest at rest, check the sensor fit, and check cabin O2 and CO2 if you can.
action.red: Tell the crew medical officer / ground medical, and check the cabin atmosphere.

explain.how: Rest a fingertip on the optical sensor and hold still. Motion and a loose fit make the reading unreliable.
explain.meaning: The share of your blood carrying oxygen. 95% or more is expected. The tile uses the median of each minute so a single bad second cannot move it.
explain.why: Low oxygen can come from the cabin atmosphere, sleep-related changes, or illness, and it affects thinking and fatigue.

metrics.title: Blood pressure
metrics.baseline_rule: median of your last logged readings in the same posture (at least 3 logs, last 30 days)

tiers.green: below 130/80 and within about 10 mmHg systolic of your baseline; for the low end at least 90/60, within about 20 mmHg of baseline, no symptoms
tiers.yellow: 130-139/80-89, a first reading of 140/90 or more, below 90/60 without symptoms, a mean arterial pressure below 65, or 20 mmHg or more below your baseline
tiers.red: 140/90 or more on repeat, 180/120 or more, any reading with chest pain, neurological symptoms or fainting, below 90/60 with dizziness or near-fainting, or a mean arterial pressure below 65 on repeat

metrics.persistence: a repeat means a second reading within 24 hours; a reading with unconfirmed technique can reach at most yellow on the numbers alone
metrics.evidence_note: The categories follow the 2025 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline. The tiers, the low-pressure limits and the baseline comparison are our own heuristic. A severe threshold of 180/120 is quoted from a secondary source and should be confirmed in the guideline.
metrics.limitation: Earth categories describe long-term risk. In flight a lower baseline is expected, and fit people often run low without symptoms. A manual reading is only as good as the technique.

action.yellow: Rest, recheck after 5 minutes with the arm at heart level, and review hydration and intake.
action.red: Lie down, then tell the crew medical officer / ground medical now.

explain.how: Sit or lie quietly for 5 minutes, support the arm at heart level, then log the cuff reading, your heart rate, your posture and any symptoms.
explain.meaning: Systolic over diastolic pressure. The mean arterial pressure (MAP = two thirds diastolic plus one third systolic) shows how well organs are perfused.
explain.why: Fluid shifts in microgravity change blood pressure. Low pressure with symptoms, or a sharp rise, needs a person to look at it.

metrics.title: Sleep
metrics.baseline_rule: 7-day average of logged nights (at least 3 nights)
metrics.evidence_note: Adults need 7-9 hours. ISS crews are scheduled about 8.5 hours but have historically averaged about 6 hours, which degrades vigilance and mood. Red below 6 hours would flag the typical ISS astronaut. That is intentional.
metrics.limitation: Logged by hand, so it is only as accurate as your entry. It is not derived from the band yet.

action.yellow: Protect your sleep window, dim lights before bed, and review the schedule.
action.red: Ask for a schedule and lighting review: tell the crew medical officer / ground medical.

explain.how: Log when you went to bed and when you woke up, and rate how well you slept.
explain.meaning: Your average sleep over the last 7 nights.
explain.why: Short sleep slows reactions, lowers mood and weakens the immune system. About six hours a night, for weeks, is enough to show.

metrics.title: Orthostatic check
metrics.baseline_rule: none (compares standing with lying down in the same check)

tiers.green: systolic drops less than 20 mmHg and diastolic less than 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing
tiers.yellow: a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic or more, without symptoms
tiers.red: the same drop with dizziness, near-fainting, confusion or blurred vision, or any fainting

metrics.evidence_note: The definition of orthostatic hypotension is clinical. Applying it to Moon and Mars gravity is our hypothesis: no partial-gravity data was found. About 20% of astronauts have presyncope after 10-14 day flights.
metrics.limitation: Standing is meaningless in microgravity, so this check is only enabled in environments with gravity and when returning to gravity.

action.yellow: Lie down, recheck in about 5 minutes, and review hydration and intake.
action.red: Lie down with your legs raised, then tell the crew medical officer / ground medical and escalate per protocol.

explain.how: Lie flat for 5 minutes and take a reading, stand up and take readings after 1 and after 3 minutes. Have something to hold on to.
explain.meaning: How much your blood pressure falls when you stand. A small heart-rate rise with a big drop, or a very big rise, is flagged as well.
explain.why: Returning to gravity after weeks in space often brings dizziness on standing. It matters most on the Moon, on Mars and on return.

metrics.title: Symptoms

tiers.green: nothing reported in the last 12 hours
tiers.yellow: a symptom of severity 3 or more reported in the last 12 hours
tiers.red: chest pain, fainting or a sudden vision change reported in the last 12 hours, at any severity

metrics.evidence_note: The symptom list is our own design, not a validated instrument.
metrics.limitation: Only reflects what you log. A quiet log means nothing was reported, not that nothing is wrong.

action.yellow: Note when it started, rest, and keep logging how it changes.
action.red: Tell the crew medical officer / ground medical now.

explain.how: Pick the symptom from the list on the Symptom Log page and rate how strong it is.
explain.meaning: A few symptoms are always worth a human's attention, however mild.
explain.why: Chest pain, fainting and a sudden change in vision can be signs of something serious, and no wearable can see them.

symptoms.label: Headache
symptoms.hint: If a cabin CO2 reading is available, check it.

log_symptoms.label: Weakness, speech or other neurological symptoms

rules.title: Possible volume loss or infection
rules.when: Low blood pressure, an elevated resting heart rate, and a raised skin temperature (or a core temperature of 38 °C or more) together.
rules.action: Lie down, drink if you can, take a core temperature, and tell the crew medical officer / ground medical now: these three together are escalated faster than any one alone.

rules.title: Crew-stress flag
rules.when: Short sleep, an elevated resting heart rate and a low WHO-5 score.

rules.title: Low SpO2 with low cabin oxygen
rules.when: Low blood oxygen while the cabin oxygen partial pressure is also low: the environmental alarm comes first.

rules.title: Headache and cabin CO2
rules.when: A headache is logged: show the cabin CO2 reading.

rules.title: Defer a safety-critical task
rules.when: Very sleepy (KSS 8 or more) or a worsening reaction test before a safety-critical task.
rules.inactive_reason: Needs the KSS and the reaction test (phase 2).

rules.title: Feeling alert, performing poorly
rules.when: The sleepiness scale says alert but the reaction test is poor: performance may be worse than it feels.
rules.inactive_reason: Needs the KSS and the reaction test (phase 2).
